summary: FeatLens builds an offline feature index by clustering functions, using static call/import relations and embeddings, and LLM-summarising each cluster into a feature description. At generation time it retrieves matching features, builds a small task-specific seed graph, and ranks dependencies with personalized PageRank, without LLM calls during retrieval. Evaluated on Python repo-level benchmarks DevEval (retrieval + generation) and EvoCodeBench (retrieval only) against BM25, UniXcoder, RepoGraph and CodexGraph.

claims.claim: FeatLens achieves the best DR@15 (0.501 DevEval, 0.460 EvoCodeBench).
claims.evidence: Fig. 3 and §5.1.1: DevEval DR@10/15/20 0.461/0.501/0.517 vs CodexGraph best 0.466 at DR@20, UniXcoder 0.415 at DR@15. RepoGraph at 0.127-0.129 looks like a poorly configured baseline (authors attribute it to LLM search-term quality). Single deterministic run, no variance.

claims.claim: Highest DIR@1 (52.91% DeepSeek-V3.2, 53.58% GPT-5-mini) with competitive Pass@1.
claims.evidence: Table 3 confirms DIR@1. Pass@1 is not better than simple dense RAG: DeepSeek 42.24 vs UniXcoder 41.40 and CodexGraph 42.31; GPT-5-mini 55.03 vs CodexGraph 56.35 and UniXcoder 53.43. Functional gains over dense retrieval are therefore ~1pp. DIR is the authors' preferred reuse metric.

claims.claim: Compared with CodexGraph, reduces nodes 61.0%, edges 86.2%, total token overhead 45.9%, with no retrieval-time LLM tokens.
claims.evidence: Table 4: 15 vs 38.5 nodes, 13.7 vs 99.3 edges, 0+7057.4 vs 3851.3+9189.6 tokens. The comparison excludes the offline LLM-based feature indexing (269-317 s and USD 0.21-0.30 per repo, Table 2/§4.1) and index maintenance under code change.
No ablation; §6.1 states results 'do not isolate the contribution of each stage'.

patterns.note: Task-local, on-demand code graph beats persistent whole-repo graphs (RepoGraph, CodexGraph) on recall and token cost, Python benchmarks only.
Static call/import extraction and deterministic PageRank ranking replace LLM-driven exploration at retrieval time.
Uses embeddings for feature matching; plain UniXcoder dense RAG nearly matches FeatLens on Pass@1.
Reports per-task token overhead and offline indexing cost.

methodology.sample: 90 DevEval projects (retrieval + generation) and 5 EvoCodeBench projects (retrieval only), filtered to those with complete dependency annotations.
methodology.baselines: No-context, BM25, UniXcoder, RepoGraph, CodexGraph. No agentic-exploration baseline (e.g., an agent with grep/LSP), the default in current coding hosts.
methodology.models: deepseek-v3.2-251201 and gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07, temperature 0, reasoning disabled.
methodology.variance: None reported; single run per configuration.
methodology.ablations: Top-N sensitivity only; no stage ablation.
methodology.contamination_controls: None discussed; DevEval/EvoCodeBench repos are public GitHub projects.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint; no venue in comment or journal_ref.
standards.artifacts: No code or data link in text.

biases.detail: Both benchmarks are Python; acknowledged in §6.2.
RepoGraph recall ~0.13 is far below even BM25 (0.30), suggesting a poor configuration; no agentic grep/LSP baseline.
Headline emphasises DR/DIR (reuse) while Pass@1 is not better than dense RAG or CodexGraph.
45.9% token saving excludes offline LLM indexing cost and index refresh.

coi.funding: No acknowledgments or funding statement found.
coi.detail: Academic group evaluating its own method; the indexing procedure adapts prior feature-summarisation work [22], likely from a related group, a mild intellectual stake.

verdict_reason: Retrieval-recall and token-overhead numbers match the tables. However, the functional gains over plain dense RAG are about 1pp, there is no stage ablation, no variance and no code, the evaluation is Python-only, one graph baseline looks broken, and the efficiency comparison omits offline LLM indexing cost.
applicability: Moderately useful as a design idea for the Java team: a feature-level index that maps business features (e.g., 'course module ingestion', 'learner content delivery') to functions, combined with static call graphs, could help agents find reusable code across ≥4 ingestion repos without whole-repo graph maintenance. Feature descriptions could also link to spec-driven development specs. The evidence does not transfer directly: Python only; Java's DI/Spring wiring and reflection are exactly the 'runtime dynamic binding and implicit framework conventions' the authors say weaken retrieval; single-repo tasks only; and no comparison against what mixed agent hosts already do (agentic grep/LSP). Treat it as a hypothesis to pilot, not a selection basis.

conflicts_with.detail: Agreement in direction: both report structure-aware graph retrieval outperforming plain vector RAG for code (there in an enterprise Java-to-microservice migration setting).
